the formation of new atmospheric aerosol particles in an iodine oxide-rich coastal environment proceeds via a two-step process, with initial cluster formation via the sequential addition of HIOD3, followed by growth via the addition of iodine oxides, with a key role played by the recycling of water either within the clusters or in the atmosphere.

the formation and growth of new aerosol in coastal environments is dominated by the sequential addition of iodine oxoacid molecules, with the subsequent formation of I2O5 clusters, which can be followed by further growth by the uptake of water vapour.

the nucleation of iodine oxide vapors, in the form of HIO3 and H2I2O4, is the primary mechanism for new particle formation at Mace Head.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the nucleation of particles from the vapours of sulfuric acid, iodine oxides, and organic compounds is a complex process that is driven by multiple pathways, which can be identified and studied in the laboratory and in the atmosphere.
the molecular-level details of nucleation in the atmosphere are not as simple as previously thought.
